The derivatives of the objective come from the sensitivities of the ODE solution and the chain rule
through every function object, without finite differences. Guide:
[Sensitivities](guide-sensitivities.html); integrators: [cppDE](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/).

| sweep | returns |
|---|---|
| forward | gradient, Gauss-Newton Hessian |
| forward over forward | exact Hessian |
| reverse | gradient |
| forward over reverse | exact Hessian |

## Forward sensitivities

The sensitivities $S = \partial x / \partial \theta$ of $\dot x = f(x, \theta)$,
$x(t_0) = x_0(\theta)$, solve

$$\dot S = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, S + \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}, \qquad
  S(t_0) = \frac{\partial x_0}{\partial \theta}, \tag{1}$$

$n_x n_\theta$ further equations. cppDE evaluates $f$ on dual numbers, one tangent per parameter,
and steps states and tangents together. The step-size control includes the tangents (`sensErrCon`),
so the sensitivities are as accurate as the states
([forward sensitivities](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-forward.html)). An event
passes the tangents through the saltation matrix of the jump
([events](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-events.html)). Every further function
object of `g*x*p` multiplies by the Jacobian of that object, e.g. $g_x S + g_\theta$ for
$y = g(x, \theta)$.

## Gradient and Hessian of the objective

Each data point adds, up to a constant,

$$\ell_j = r_j^2 + \log \sigma_j^2, \qquad r_j = \frac{g_j - y_j}{\sigma_j}, \tag{2}$$

the summand of [the data term](methods-objective.html#data-term). For fixed $\sigma_j$ and
$J = \partial r / \partial \theta$, the gradient is $2 J^\top r$ and the Hessian

$$\nabla^2 \sum_j r_j^2 = 2 J^\top J + 2 \sum_j r_j\, \nabla^2 r_j . \tag{3}$$

The Gauss-Newton term $2 J^\top J$ is positive semidefinite and needs first-order sensitivities;
the second term matters for large residuals or strong nonlinearity.

### Gauss-Newton with an error model

For $\sigma_j(\theta)$, the Hessian of $\ell_j$ in $(g_j, \sigma_j)$ is

$$L_j = \frac{2}{\sigma_j^2} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 r_j \\ -2 r_j & 3 r_j^2 - 1 \end{pmatrix},
  \qquad \det L_j = -\frac{4\,(1 + r_j^2)}{\sigma_j^4} < 0. \tag{4}$$

The Gauss-Newton Hessian of `normL2()` is $\sum_j J_j^\top L_j J_j$, $J_j$ the Jacobian of
$(g_j, \sigma_j)$: exact curvature of $\ell_j$, no second derivatives of $g_j$ and $\sigma_j$. By (4)
$L_j$ has one negative eigenvalue at every residual, and the $\sigma\sigma$ entry $3 r_j^2 - 1$ is
negative where residuals are small, so the matrix is in general indefinite along directions that
move a sigma. The exact Hessian adds the
second derivatives of $g_j$ and $\sigma_j$, weighted by $2 r_j / \sigma_j$ and
$2 (1 - r_j^2) / \sigma_j$.

## Forward over forward

Differentiating (1) again gives $n_x n_\theta (n_\theta + 1) / 2$ equations and the exact Hessian,
for small models.

## Reverse sweep

The gradient of the objective alone follows from one backward sweep with the multipliers
$\lambda(t)$, zero after the last measurement, and the terms $\ell_j$ of the data at the
measurement times $t_j$,

$$\begin{aligned}
\dot\lambda &= -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\top} \lambda, \qquad
\lambda(t_j^-) = \lambda(t_j^+) + \left(\frac{\partial \ell_j}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\top}, \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}(-2 \log L)}{\mathrm{d}\theta} &= \int \lambda^\top \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\,
\mathrm{d}t + \lambda(t_0)^\top \frac{\partial x_0}{\partial \theta}
+ \sum_j \frac{\partial \ell_j}{\partial \theta} .
\end{aligned} \tag{5}$$

cppDE uses the *discrete adjoint* of the
integrator steps, the exact derivative of the computed objective, with checkpoints of the forward
trajectory ([reverse mode](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-reverse.html)). The
cost is a few times the value, independent of $n_\theta$. The value pass solves without
sensitivities, and the sweep uses the step grid of that pass. `Pimpl()` passes the sweep through
the Jacobian of the root ([Steady states](methods-steady-states.html#derivatives-of-the-root)).

### Accuracy of a reverse gradient

By default the adjoint follows the step grid of the states without error control.

| option of `optionsReverse` | effect |
|---|---|
| `refine = TRUE` | every step held to the CVODES backward error test under the solve tolerances; a failing step is swept again in substeps |
| `gradtol` | the share of each step in the gradient added to that test as absolute tolerance |

A trust region converges with a gradient whose error is small relative to the gradient
[@carter1991global; @conn2000trust]. `gradtol` bounds the error of every step in absolute terms,
and the errors of the steps add up over the sweep; near the optimum, where the gradient vanishes,
a fixed `gradtol` does not keep the relative error small
([checking the sweep](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-reverse-checks.html)).

A refined sweep differentiates the trajectory with substeps, not the computed one. Under `refine` it
therefore returns, per seed, the first-order change of the seeded functional between the two: over
the steps, the adjoint at the step end times the difference of the end states, plus the seeds times
the difference of the observed values
([value correction](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-reverse-checks.html#value-correction)).
The `normL2()` seed gives the change of the objective, a second seed the change of `chi2`. The
reverse objective adds both, so value and gradient belong to one function, and a value-only call
also sweeps. The corrected value is not necessarily closer to the exact one; accepted steps get no
correction.

## Forward over reverse

Forward tangents, one per parameter, ride on the backward sweep, which returns one Hessian column
per tangent. Cost grows like a forward solve; the $n_\theta^2$ Hessian entries are accumulated, but
no $n_x n_\theta^2$ second-order sensitivities are integrated or stored
([forward over reverse](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-forward-reverse.html)).

### Second derivatives along directions

FOCEI ([Nonlinear mixed-effects models](guide-nlme.html)) needs traces
$\operatorname{tr}(M\, \partial H_i / \partial \psi)$ for the volume term and the joint Hessian
along random-effect directions. Random effects of different groups never share a condition, so the
$k$-th random effect of all groups shares one tangent $v_k$, and one forward pass along $K$ tangents
serves all groups. A backward sweep with seed $w$ on the predictions and sigmas of the data rows,
and $\dot w_k$ along tangent $k$, returns $J^\top w$ and

$$\sum_r w_r\, \nabla^2 z_r\, v_k + J^\top \dot w_k \tag{6}$$

for every $k$, $z_r$ prediction or sigma of row $r$, $J$ their Jacobian. With the gradient of the
row loss as seed and $L_r J_r v_k$ as tangent derivative, $L_r$ the Hessian (4), the sweep gives
$\Phi_i^{\eta\eta}$, $\Phi_i^{\eta\psi}$ and the mode shift
$\mathrm{d}\hat\eta / \mathrm{d}\psi = -(\Phi_i^{\eta\eta})^{-1} \Phi_i^{\eta\psi}$. The trace
gradients are linear in $M$: seed $j$ is $2 L_r J_{r,j}$, with tangent derivative the derivative of
$L_r$ contracted with $J_{r,j}$ and $J_{r,k}$. With $U_{jk}$ slice $k$ of the result for seed $j$,

$$\nabla \operatorname{tr}(M H_i) = \sum_{j,k} M_{jk}\, U_{jk} \tag{7}$$

for every symmetric $M$: $K$ seeds for any number of matrices. Hessian rows and trace seeds go back
in one sweep, every cotangent with $K + 1$ blocks, the seed and the derivative of the seed along
each tangent.

Reference: `odemodel()`, `Xs()`, `Y()`, `P()`, `Pimpl()`, `normL2()`
